About: Newton's Third Law — Action–Reaction Pairs

Source

Lecture
Introductory classical mechanics — Newtonian dynamics (Newton's third law of motion).
Simulation
"Newton's Third Law — Action–Reaction Pairs": a single 1-D scene — two carts push off from rest, forces equal and opposite, response set by a = F/m, plus a labeled ⚠ counterfactual (F ∝ mass) for contrast.
Concept
Interaction forces come as equal-magnitude opposite pairs acting on two different bodies; each body's response is set by a = Fnet/m.
Serves
Equal & opposite pair on different bodies, recoil |aA|/|aB| = mB/mA with Σp = 0.
Inquiry
During contact, do the two force readouts differ? Does |vB|/|vA| track mA/mB as the masses change? What happens to Σp in ⚠ mode?
Misconception
"The heavier body pushes harder" — the pair is equal each way, whatever the masses; the lighter body just responds more (a = F/m).

Newton's Third Law

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet Law ③ — the push-off

Heavy cart A (4 kg) and light cart B (1 kg) rest with hands in contact. For 0.8 s they push off each other (✓ Newton). Green arrows show each velocity. Before releasing them, look at the two force arrows during contact — that pair is the whole story.

2 · Predict — the contact pair

Heavy A and light B push off from rest, hands in contact for 0.8 s (✓ Newton). During the contact, how do the forces on the two bodies compare?

3 · Watch the pair — and the getaway

▶ Play. During contact the force arrows stay equal and opposite; after release each cart keeps its velocity (Law ① at work). Check |vB| / |vA| = mA/mB = 4 in the readouts. Drag mA and push off again — does the ratio follow? Open 📊 Data: Σp stays 0.

4 · Law ③ in one line

Interaction forces come only as equal-magnitude, opposite pairs on the two different bodies — whatever the masses. The lighter body simply responds more: a = F/m. Flip ⚠ mode (F ∝ mass) and watch Σp grow during contact — real internal forces can never do that.

③ Action–reaction

F on A = −(F on B) ⇒ |a_A|/|a_B| = m_B/m_A

+5 N on B ⇒ −5 N on A, always — on the two different bodies. From rest, mAvA + mBvB = 0 (total momentum stays zero).

⚠ The counterfactual (for contrast)

F_X ∝ m_X

⚠ "Heavier pushes harder": body X pushes with 5 N·mX/m̄ — an unequal pair, so Σp is not conserved. It is implemented exactly so you can watch it fail.

01

At a glance

Two carts stand at rest on a smooth floor, with their hands touching. A heavy cart A and a light cart B push off each other for a short time and roll apart. You set the two masses.

What you'll learn

  • How to name a force by the body it acts on and the body that exerts it.
  • How the push of one cart on the other compares with the push back.
  • How a rival rule, marked ⚠ in the sim, differs from the real one.
The set-up before the push: a heavy cart A and a light cart B, a spring between their hands, and +x pointing right.

What's on screen

  • Cart A: the cyan cart on the left, with its mass in the label. The mass sets its size.
  • Cart B: the amber cart on the right.
  • Force arrows: amber arrows on each cart, drawn only during the push, 9 px for every newton.
  • Velocity arrows: green arrows above the carts, drawn once a cart moves, with the value in m/s.
  • Phase chip: the tag at the top right reads Pre-launch, Contact or Separated.
See itOpen the sim with the carts at rest at t = 0, paused. Watch for: the big cyan cart A (4 kg), the small amber cart B (1 kg), and the spring between them.

03

Every force has a body it acts on and a body that exerts it

A force is never alone: one body pushes, another body is pushed. So each force needs two names. The sim's readouts follow this rule. F on A is the force exerted on cart A by cart B. F on B is the force exerted on cart B by cart A.

The arrows on each readout give the direction. Take +x to the right, as in the figure: a force pointing left is negative, and one pointing right is positive.

  • Pre-launch (t from 0 to 0.4 s). The carts touch through the spring and both forces read 0.0 N.
  • Contact (0.4 to 1.2 s). The spring pushes, and each cart has one force acting on it along x.
  • Separated (after 1.2 s). The spring is gone, so both forces read 0.0 N again and each cart coasts.

Gravity and the floor's push act on each cart too. They are vertical and cancel, so they are not drawn.

See itRun the push-off from the start and follow the phase chip at the top right. Watch for: Pre-launch, then Contact with the spring still drawn, then Separated with both carts moving.
04

The two forces of a pair are equal and opposite

Newton's third law says that when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts a force on A that is equal in size and opposite in direction:

F⃗on A by B = −F⃗on B by A
The two forces exist together and never one without the other.

In the sim, during the contact each cart feels 5.0 N. F on A reads 5.0 N pointing left, which is −5.0 N, and F on B reads 5.0 N pointing right, +5.0 N. The two arrows are the same length. This holds whatever the masses are: a pair stays equal even when one body is much heavier than the other.

The two forces act on different bodies. This is why they never cancel: each one changes the motion of its own cart only.

See itPause the push-off in the middle of the contact. Watch for: two amber arrows of the same length, and the readouts F on A = 5.0 N ← and F on B = 5.0 N →.
05

The lighter cart gains more speed

Equal forces do not mean equal motion. Each cart answers its own force through Newton's second law, a = F/m. With 5.0 N for 0.8 s:

  • Cart A (4 kg): a = −5.0/4 = −1.25 m/s², so vA = −1.25 × 0.8 = −1.00 m/s.
  • Cart B (1 kg): a = +5.0/1 = +5.00 m/s², so vB = +5.00 × 0.8 = +4.00 m/s.
  • The force is the same, so the speeds are in the ratio of the masses, upside down: |vB| / |vA| = mA / mB = 4.00.

After the contact both forces are zero, so each cart keeps its speed.

mA mB

These sliders move the sim too.

See itSet mA = 2 kg and mB = 1 kg, run past the contact and open the Data panel. Watch for: vA = −2.00 m/s, vB = +4.00 m/s and the ratio 2.00, equal to mA / mB.
06

The total momentum stays zero

The momentum of a cart is p = m v. The total for the two carts is Σp = mAvA + mBvB. Both carts start at rest, so Σp starts at 0.

Each cart gains momentum equal to force times time, the impulse. The two forces are equal and opposite and last the same 0.8 s, so the impulses are 5.0 × 0.8 = 4.0 N·s in opposite directions.

  • mAvA = 4 × (−1.00) = −4.00 kg·m/s, and mBvB = 1 × (+4.00) = +4.00 kg·m/s.
  • They add to Σp = 0, and this holds during the contact as well as after it.
  • It holds for any masses. For mA = 8 kg and mB = 0.5 kg the speeds are −0.50 and +8.00 m/s, and Σp is still 0.

This is why a pair of internal forces cannot push the pair as a whole in either direction.

See itSet mA = 8 kg and mB = 0.5 kg, run past the contact and open the Data panel. Watch for: vA = −0.50 m/s, vB = +8.00 m/s and Σp = 0.00 kg·m/s.
07

A rule where the heavier cart pushes harder fails

The ⚠ F ∝ mass button runs a rival rule that the sim marks as wrong, so that you can watch it fail. Each cart X pushes with a force proportional to its own mass:

FX = 5 N × mX / m̄, with m̄ = (mA + mB) / 2
The pair is no longer equal and opposite, except when the masses are equal.

For 4 kg and 1 kg, m̄ = 2.5 kg, so cart A is pushed with 2.0 N and cart B with 8.0 N. After 0.8 s, vA = −0.40 m/s and vB = +6.40 m/s. The total momentum is Σp = −1.60 + 6.40 = +4.80 kg·m/s.

Two carts that started at rest and only touched each other have gained momentum from nothing. No experiment on an isolated pair has ever shown this, so a real pair must be equal and opposite.

See itSwitch to the ⚠ model with the default masses and run past the contact. Watch for: unequal arrows, 2.0 N on A and 8.0 N on B, and in the Data panel Σp = +4.80 kg·m/s.
08

Where it matters

  • Rifle recoil. A 0.010 kg bullet leaves a 4.0 kg rifle at 400 m/s. The bullet gains +4.0 kg·m/s, so the rifle gains −4.0 kg·m/s and recoils at 1.0 m/s. The gas is ignored here.
  • Walking. Your foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes your foot forward. The ground is Earth itself, so its backward shove on the planet is far too small to see.
  • Rockets. A rocket pushes its exhaust backward, and the exhaust pushes the rocket forward. This works in empty space, where there is nothing else to push against.
09

Summary

In one line. Newton's third law describes how two bodies push on each other, and how each body responds.

Key points

  • Forces come in pairs, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on two different bodies.
  • Each body responds by a = F/m, so the lighter one gains more speed: |vB| / |vA| = mA / mB.
  • Starting from rest, Σp stays 0. In the ⚠ rule it does not, so that rule fails.

Common mix-ups

  • "The heavier body pushes harder." The pair is equal each way. The heavier body just responds less.
  • "Equal and opposite forces cancel, so nothing moves." They act on different bodies, so each one moves its own body.
  • "A book's weight and the table's push on it are a pair." Both act on the book. The pair of the weight is the book's pull on Earth.

Things to try on your own

  • Set mA = mB and check that the carts leave at equal speeds.
  • Predict vB for mA = 6 kg and mB = 1.5 kg before you run it.
  • In the ⚠ model set mA = mB and see why Σp is 0 again.
